Proof Step 1

🎯 What was built

Share-buyback voting — the whole exercise, run on pitchIN.

Before

Hundreds of votes collected in a Google Form — reconciled by hand, drifting out of sync with platform holdings and records.

Now

Voters, payouts, votes and the published result run on-platform, tied to live shareholder data — all at once, no desync.

Why it matters

A new post-fundraising service pitchIN can offer issuers — extending the platform's value beyond the raise.

One maker–checker flow across three apps: Admin creates the buyback and uploads the voter list → SuperAdmin approves → investors see their payout and vote → the result is published to the company's Announcements tab. The platform tallies; a human decides — pitchIN is the nominee (ADR-0001).

Proof Step 2

🔁 The maker–checker feature flow

Who does what, in order. The separation is deliberate: the person who creates an action is never the person who approves or publishes it, and the platform only ever tallies — a human makes the call.

Admin (maker) SuperAdmin (checker) Investor
Why QA cares

The control that matters most — investors never see tally numbers — is asserted by an automated smoke test (see §7). The maker ≠ checker split is enforced by the two separate approval/publish roles.

De-risk Step 3

🔍 Review it yourselves — without us touching staging

Everything you need to review this yourselves is pre-staged — no back-and-forth with Nicholas required. Pick your depth:

Option A — Run it locally from the private review repos recommended

The four repos are pushed to temporary private repos on Nicholas's GitHub (nicholas@pitchin.my), prefixed corporate-actions-review-* — you're invited as collaborators, and the default branch is already nicholas-ralph (the feature). The test repo also carries the QA harness, the docker-compose infra, and the seed bootstrap, so a full local run needs nothing from the workspace. Official staging is never touched.

Why a temp repo, not a fork

pitchIN's GitHub org doesn't allow forking of private repositories, so the work sits in throwaway private repos on Nicholas's account instead. They'll be deleted once the review is done — deleting them removes the copies and revokes access automatically.

# clone each review repo (URLs in the case study's Reviewer Pack), e.g.:
git clone github.com/ncih-pitchin/corporate-actions-review-pitchinAPI   # lands on nicholas-ralph

# bring the stack up + run the local QA gates:
docker compose -f infra/docker-compose.yml up -d   # Postgres + Azurite + RabbitMQ
# … boot API + customer web per SETUP.md …
bin/local-qa.sh                    # checks the stack, runs Playwright PW_ENV=local

The repo URLs, copy-paste bring-up, harness and seed data are all collected in one place — the Reviewer Pack in the case study (linked below). Detail: SETUP.md · docs/HOW-TO-RUN-LOCAL-QA.md.

Option B — Zero-hosting: a git bundle

Prefer nothing hosted at all? Each repo is also available as a single bundle file you clone directly — same source, no GitHub:

git clone CorporateActions-pitchinAPI.bundle    # one self-contained file per repo

Option C — Fastest, no setup: just look

The published case study (13 real screenshots) and the clickable walkthrough let you review the whole journey in a browser with nothing to install.

Everything in one place

The case study has a Reviewer Pack section with the fork URLs, the bundle downloads, the harness, the seed data, and the exact run commands — your one self-serve entry point.

De-risk Step 4

⚙️ How it was built — the AI pipeline (with human gates)

The agent doesn't free-wheel. Work runs through a disciplined pipeline driven off the GitHub issue tracker, with a human verification gate before anything closes and money/KYC/settlement always deferred to a human.

Owner AI agent Human-confirmed step / gate Your normal pipeline

Skills: grill-with-docs → to-prd → to-issues → triage → tdd → human-verify → ship. A human confirms the issue breakdown (step 4) and the triage labels (step 5) before the agent builds — and verifies every ticket (step 8) before anything closes.

The ask Step 5

📦 Exactly what gets pushed

Today the feature lives on one local branch (nicholas-ralph), pushed nowhere. That branch mixes two things: the product feature and a handful of local "carries" — ~40 lines of laptop-only plumbing (a DB seed toggle, a cache table, a local API port, a dev SSL cert) that let the app boot on a Mac. The carries must never reach production.

The clean-up is a standard rebase that lifts only the feature commits onto each repo's real branch and leaves the carries behind — producing one ordinary, product-only PR per repo:

RepoLands onFeature commitsWhat it isRisk
pitchinWebTestScriptsmain2The e2e + smoke specs & page objects (test-only)lowest
pitchinAPIstaging_v824New CorporateActions module (~1,950-line service · 3 controllers · 6 EF migrations · ~2,000 lines of tests)medium
PitchinAdminWebstaging15Admin CA screens · service · i18nmedium
PitchinCustomerWebstaging~18Investor vote modal · detail page · announcement feed (drop 2 dev-cert commits)medium

What's new vs what's edited

Most of the change is new, self-contained code — the edits to existing files are small and mechanical (wiring, routing, translations), which keeps the review surface low.

  • pitchinAPI — New: a self-contained CorporateActions module (entities, ~1,950-line service, DTOs, 3 controllers, 6 migrations, tests). Edited: only the wiring to register it (DI / module).
  • PitchinAdminWeb — New: the CA screens + corporate-actions.service.ts. Edited: routing/nav menu + i18n string files.
  • PitchinCustomerWeb — New: the investor vote modal, CA detail page, the unwrapResult() helper. Edited: the existing announcement feed (to surface the result) + market-details. ⚠ Drop the 2 dev-cert commits; sanity-check the "Thank you" page commit.
  • pitchinWebTestScripts — New (test-only): the e2e + smoke specs, page objects, voter-file util.

How granular do you want the push?

The work naturally splits by repo (4 PRs), but you decide how to sequence the review. Three options:

OptionWhat it meansTrade-off
1 · One coordinated drop recommendedAll four PRs opened together and reviewed as one feature, merged in dependency order (test + API first, then the two web apps).Reviewed as a coherent whole — the feature is cross-app, so the pieces make most sense seen together; one review session.
2 · Staged by riskLand the test-only PR first, then the API, then the web apps over separate sessions.Lowest blast radius per step, but stretches the review across several rounds and splits the feature's context.
3 · Per-issue micro-PRsSplit each repo's commits back into the ~21 underlying tickets.Most granular, but the feature is cross-app — many tickets span repos and don't split cleanly. Usually more review overhead, not less.
Recommendation for the meeting

One coordinated drop: open all four PRs together and review them as a single feature, since the work spans the three apps and reads best as a whole. Merge in dependency order — the test-only and API PRs first, then the two web apps. (The test-only PR carries zero product risk and lets QA wire the automated gate into CI.)

Safety net Step 6

🛡️ How production stays safe

This is the core claim of the whole POC, and it's structural — not a promise:

  • The PRs contain only product code. None of the AI setup — the agent skills, the local infra, the domain docs — goes into a product repo. It lives in a separate workspace folder that isn't even a git repo, so it can't leak into a PR.
  • The pipeline is untouched. Reviewers and CI see a completely standard change — branch → PR → review → existing CI gates → merge. Same process as any human PR.
  • The laptop "carries" are left behind by the rebase — the DB-seed toggle, local port and dev cert never reach staging.
  • Money / KYC / settlement code is out of scope. The agent is instructed to defer all of it to a human; Corporate Actions touches none of those rails.
  • A human verified every ticket before it was considered done, and QA gates it again before staging (§7).
The honest caveat

The API test suite has a known red baseline (564 pass / 632 fail) — but all failures are test-side (mocking limitations), not product bugs; the app boots and serves. The gate for this work is "no new failures beyond baseline," and the Corporate Actions tests are green. Cleaning that baseline is a separate, test-only task.

Frontend QA rule

A green production build does not prove a screen renders correctly. A frontend criterion is only "verified" when its render smoke ran (PW_ENV=local … -g @smoke); otherwise it routes to human UAT. The implementer never edits the test that grades its own UI (ADR-0009).

Safety net Step 8

🧰 QA infrastructure already prepared

What this is — and isn't

Everything below was built for local testing and experimentation during the POC — to prove the feature works on a laptop. It's not a prerequisite for you to adopt. But it's here, it works, and you're welcome to reuse any of it if it's useful to QA.

  • One-command local e2e — bin/local-qa.sh checks the stack is up and runs Playwright (PW_ENV=local, never staging). Entry point: docs/HOW-TO-RUN-LOCAL-QA.md.
  • Corporate Actions specs — corporateAction.e2e.spec.ts (full 6-step cross-app journey, driven to a real green run) and corporateAction.smoke.spec.ts (investor render tracer; asserts investors never see tally numbers).
  • Page objects + util — corporateAction.page.ts, adminCorporateAction.page.ts, and voterFile.ts (generates the voter Excel).
  • Seed data / bootstrap — local-bootstrap/ fabricates the test world on demand (campaigns, verified/funded investors, PSTX orders) so a journey runs from an empty local DB. Specs also create/find by ID (ADR-0002), so they're self-contained and rerunnable. The same harness already runs the money journeys (ECF/PSTX) green locally.
  • Guardrails — the screen-smoke tier, the unwrapResult() operator, ADR-0009 (an agent never grades its own UI), and a living VERIFICATION-CHECKLIST.md of "green-but-broken" traps (EF no-tracking silent save, unregistered migration, hash routing, …).
Reusable by QA

If it's useful, the pieces worth keeping regardless of the AI work: the one-command local gate, the seed/bootstrap (so anyone gets a runnable local world from empty), the screen-smoke tier (catches "renders-but-broken" that a green build misses), and the traps checklist. Independent of the POC — adopt any subset.

Beyond this feature

🚀 What's next

Corporate Actions is the first real, multi-issue feature the AI build loop has shipped end-to-end (every ticket human-verified). If this push goes well, the scale-up path is:

  • A fully unattended end-to-end run. So far a human verified every ticket; the open next step is a single, hands-off run from issue → verified PR on a low-risk, well-specified ticket.
  • Clean the red test baseline (the 582 ClickUp-mock failures) — test-only, low risk — so automated verification is fully green and we can trust the agent on more unattended.
  • More epics through the same pipeline — each one an ordinary, clean PR; the pipeline never changes.
  • On buy-in, publish the AI setup to a dedicated pitchin-ai repo and share it with the team, so everyone codes with the same guardrails.

The full POC narrative — environment bring-up, roadblocks, the honest AI-readiness assessment — is in the case study and the POC report that accompany this deck.
